speaker: Pat
text: Thanks for coming over. I know the bill is why we're all here, so let's start there. Where would you like to begin?

speaker: Sandy
text: Where would I like to begin? With you paying the one point four million the contract says you owe us. That's where I begin.

speaker: Riley
text: Your project manager changed the spec to solid oak. That's how you got to one point four. And now you're pretending you never heard of it. That's not honest, and you know it.

speaker: Morgan
text: Then pay it. It's not complicated. You changed the order, we built what you asked for, and the invoice is due in fifteen days.

speaker: Sam
text: Fifteen days. Okay. Is that the oak supplier's deadline, or the bank's?

speaker: Sandy
text: Does it matter whose deadline it is? You're stalling. Every question you ask is another day I don't have.

speaker: Jordan
text: I hear you. You're under real time pressure and we're asking a lot of questions. We're not stalling; we're trying to understand the number before we respond to it.

speaker: Riley
text: Understand the number? It's on the invoice you were sent three weeks ago. There is nothing to understand.

speaker: Pat
text: Okay. Let's take the invoice as read. What happens on your side if it isn't paid in full on day fifteen?

speaker: Sandy
text: What happens is we go under. The oak supplier doesn't wait, the bank doesn't wait, and I lose the house my kids grew up in. Is that what you want? Is that the plan?

speaker: Sam
text: No. Nobody on this side wants you to go under. That would be worse for us too: we don't get the loan back, and we lose the best carpentry crew we've worked with.

speaker: Morgan
text: Then stop treating us like we're trying to rob you. Pay the bill. You have the money; you're out there buying hotels.

speaker: Jordan
text: Can we set the question of who owes what aside for a minute and look at what we can actually do in the next fifteen days?

speaker: Sandy
text: No, we can't set it aside. That's the whole point. You did the same thing on the Elm Street job: change the subject until the other side gives up.

speaker: Pat
text: That's fair; you're entitled to be angry about how this was handled, and I'm sorry we're in this spot. Tell me what's bothering you most about it.

speaker: Sandy
text: What's bothering me most? That I trusted your people. Fawn said 'go ahead', we went ahead, and now I'm the one facing a trustee. You put me here.

speaker: Morgan
text: And frankly, if you'd read your own project manager's emails you'd have known about the oak in March. Don't put that on us.

speaker: Sam
text: We're not putting it on you. I want to make sure I understand the sequence, though: Fawn emailed in March, the oak went in over the summer, and the invoice landed three weeks ago. Is that right?

speaker: Sandy
text: That's right. And every week of those, your office had the invoice and said nothing. Nothing! You waited until we were out of room to start asking questions.

speaker: Riley
text: Which is exactly what someone does when they want the other side to fold. So don't tell us you're trying to understand.

speaker: Pat
text: I'm not going to tell you what to think about our motives. I'd rather show you. Jordan, what can we actually put on the table today?

speaker: Jordan
text: We can pay two hundred thousand this week against the invoice, no strings. That's cash we have. The rest we need to talk about.

speaker: Sandy
text: Two hundred. Out of one point four. That's an insult, and you know it.

speaker: Morgan
text: It's not even the loan amount. Come on.

speaker: Sam
text: I know it's a long way from the total. It's what we can move this week without touching the hotel deposit. Help me understand which matters more to you right now: the size of the first payment, or the certainty that the supplier gets paid on day fifteen?

speaker: Sandy
text: The supplier. If the supplier's one point one is paid on day fifteen, I'm still in business. If it isn't, the rest of this conversation is academic.

speaker: Pat
text: So one point one to the supplier by day fifteen is the line that can't move, and the remaining three hundred is where there's room. Have I got that right?

speaker: Riley
text: Yes. That's it.

speaker: Jordan
text: Then here's a shape. Two hundred this week, and we go with you to the supplier and guarantee the remaining nine hundred on day fifteen; our bank will do that against the lakefront deal. The three hundred we settle over six months, with the rent as the offset.

speaker: Sandy
text: You'd guarantee it in writing? Before day fifteen?

speaker: Pat
text: In writing, this week. Sam will draft it tonight.

speaker: Riley
text: Okay. Okay. I'm sorry about the 'robbing you' stuff. That was the morning talking.

speaker: Sandy
text: And the future work, the hotel: is that a real conversation or a carrot?

speaker: Pat
text: Real. If we come out of this with you still standing, you're the crew I want on the hotel. We can put a letter of intent in the same envelope.

speaker: Jordan
text: So to sum up: two hundred this week, a written guarantee for nine hundred to the supplier on day fifteen, three hundred over six months against the rent, and a letter of intent on the hotel. Anything I've missed?

speaker: Sandy
text: No. That's the whole thing. Thank you.
